name: Warm Brown
lede: Warm Brown is a descriptive name for an orange-leaning brown, and the books show where such browns came from: iron earths, umber, sepia ink and the glazes of old painters.

sections.title: A description with a long record
sections.body: Warm brown is a survey-style name, taken here from the xkcd color survey, and not a historical color word [1]. The phrase itself, though, turns up in writing about paint, where Ball uses it for Rembrandt's browns and the Compendium for umber [2][3]. The swatch is a strong orange-brown, nearest to [[chocolate]] [1].

sections.title: What made warm browns
sections.body:
Most of them were earths. The Compendium puts manganese oxides at 5 to 20 per cent in umbers and under 10 per cent in siennas, and calls umbers a rich, warm brown [3]. Prehistoric cave paintings of cattle and deer got their warm browns and maroons from such earth pigments [4]. Sepia, a deep warm brown, was made from the ink of the cuttlefish, whose dark color comes from melanin, and the ink was used for writing from Roman times until the nineteenth century [5].

Lignite, a soft brown coal, gives a transparent warm brown pigment close to umber, but it may fade in sunlight [6]. See also [[umber]], [[sienna]] and [[sepia]].

sections.title: Rembrandt's browns
sections.body: Ball, following the conservator Doerner, says Rembrandt painted deep shadows and golden light, under which everything turned to warm browns that he made beautiful [2]. They were not simple. In *An Elderly Man as St Paul* (about 1659), the book's cover is not umber at all but a thin glaze built of lakes, earth reds and yellows, and bone black [2]. Later, lesser painters made the same brownness a convention, the hue of art made to please conservative patrons [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive has 342 paintings among 23,781 in which this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas, within six color-distance units [7]. The color is most over-represented in the 1400s, at about 1.7 times its overall rate, and nearly absent in the 1900s, at 0.3 times [7]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the browns are partly the work of time [7].
